prompt: What happens to a packet that matches no entry in a nonempty ordinary IPv4 interface ACL?
options: It is denied by the implicit final rule
It uses the action of the preceding matching flow
It is permitted when the route is directly connected
It is evaluated only against the opposite direction
explanation: Every nonempty ACL ends with an implicit deny any, so a packet that matches no entry is dropped. Routes and earlier flows do not change that.

whyWrong.1: An ordinary ACL decides each packet on its own.
whyWrong.2: A connected route does not override an ACL deny.
whyWrong.3: A packet is checked only in the direction it travels.

prompt: Which two numbers identify standard IPv4 ACLs on IOS? Choose two.
explanation: Standard IPv4 ACL numbers are 1–99 and 1300–1999, so 99 and 1400 are standard.

whyWrong.1: 150 is in the extended range 100–199.
whyWrong.3: 2300 is in the extended range 2000–2699.

prompt: On classic IOS, CLIENTS-IN has not been created. What filtering does `ip access-group CLIENTS-IN in` provide?
options: Implicit deny applies before any entry is created
The last previously attached list remains selected
An absent reference leaves this IPv4 path unfiltered
The empty list inherits the opposite direction's rules
explanation: IOS permits all traffic through a referenced ACL that does not exist or is empty. A misspelled name therefore leaves the interface unfiltered.

whyWrong.0: The implicit deny applies only to a list that has entries.
whyWrong.1: The reference names this list; no earlier list stays active.
whyWrong.3: Inbound and outbound attachments do not share entries.

exhibit.title: Representative interface and ACL excerpts
exhibit.text:
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound access list is not set
R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
  10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
  20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
  30 permit ip any any

prompt: The ACL was meant to filter traffic from clients arriving on G0/0. What fault does this output show?
options: No IPv4 interface ACL is attached to G0/0
A broad permit is ahead of the specific deny
The ACL is attached outbound on G0/0
Counters must be cleared before the list can filter
explanation: The output shows no inbound or outbound ACL on G0/0. Creating an ACL does nothing until `ip access-group` attaches it.

whyWrong.1: The shown list has its specific entries before the broad permit.
whyWrong.2: The outbound direction also shows not set.
whyWrong.3: Clearing counters does not activate filtering.

prompt: Which two statements are correct for ordinary routed IPv4 interface ACLs? Choose two.
options: One IPv4 list can be attached in each interface direction
Two inbound list names form a combined ordered filter
An inbound attachment also checks replies leaving that interface
A host transit test avoids assuming a router ping follows that path
An outbound permit overrides an inbound deny on the same router
explanation: An interface can have one IPv4 ACL per direction. A ping from the router itself can take a different path, so test transit policy from a host.

whyWrong.1: A second inbound reference replaces the first.
whyWrong.2: An inbound ACL checks only packets arriving on the interface; replies leaving are outbound.
whyWrong.4: A packet denied inbound never reaches an outbound permit.

prompt: Which two statements about the TCP `established` keyword are correct? Choose two.
options: It checks that the segment belongs to a stored connection
It accepts a TCP segment carrying ACK or RST
It requires the initial client SYN to have been observed
It can match a forged ACK without a previous connection
It applies the same return-session test to UDP replies
explanation: `established` matches TCP segments with the ACK or RST flag set. It does not track connections, so a forged ACK packet also matches.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary ACLs keep no connection table.
whyWrong.2: It tests the flags in the current packet and does not remember a SYN.
whyWrong.4: UDP has no ACK or RST flags.

prompt: R1 has VTY lines 0–4. Which command under those lines limits incoming management sessions to sources in standard ACL 10?
options: ip access-group 10 in
transport input 10
access-class 10 out
access-class 10 in
explanation: `access-class 10 in` applies the ACL to incoming VTY connections. It does not enable SSH or check passwords.

whyWrong.0: `ip access-group` is an interface command, not a line command.
whyWrong.1: `transport input` selects protocols such as ssh, not an ACL.
whyWrong.2: `out` applies to outgoing connections, not incoming sessions.

prompt: CLIENTS-IN is applied inbound on R1 G0/0, facing 10.100.10.0/24. Which entry first matches an ICMP echo request from 10.100.10.11 to 10.100.20.20?
options: 10: the destination is the web server
15: this entry matches the ICMP protocol
20: neither earlier entry matches every field
30: the final permit overrides earlier denies
explanation: Entry 10 requires TCP, so the ICMP packet misses it. Entry 15 requires source .10, not .11, so the packet first matches deny 20.

whyWrong.0: The destination matches, but entry 10 also requires TCP.
whyWrong.1: The source is .11, not .10, so entry 15 does not match.
whyWrong.3: The first match ends evaluation, so a later permit cannot override it.

prompt: With base address 172.16.32.0, which wildcard matches exactly the /20 subnet?
explanation: A /20 mask is 255.255.240.0, and 255.255.255.255 minus that is the wildcard 0.0.15.255. It covers third octets 32 through 47.

whyWrong.0: 0.0.31.255 ignores five third-octet bits and matches a /19.
whyWrong.1: 16 is the block size, not the wildcard value.
whyWrong.3: 0.0.255.255 ignores two octets and matches the whole /16.

prompt: Which source range matches the displayed entry?
explanation: Wildcard 7 is binary 00000111, so the third octet can range from 16 to 23. The wildcard 255 in the last octet matches any host value.

whyWrong.2: The compared high bits keep the third octet within 16–23.
whyWrong.3: That range would need wildcard 0.0.15.255.

exhibit.title: Representative effective ACL order
exhibit.text:
access-list 101 permit ip any any
access-list 101 deny tcp any host 10.100.20.30 eq 22

prompt: ACL 101 is applied inbound where clients' requests arrive. The goal is to block SSH to 10.100.20.30 and permit other IPv4 traffic. Why is SSH still permitted?
options: The final deny overrides the permit only after counters are cleared
Adding established to the deny will catch the initial SYN
The more specific deny should win regardless of sequence
The broad permit accepts SSH before the deny is evaluated
explanation: The first entry permits all IPv4 packets, including SSH, so the deny is never reached. ACLs use the first match, so the specific deny must come first.

whyWrong.0: Clearing counters does not change the order of evaluation.
whyWrong.1: A new SSH SYN has no ACK or RST, so `established` would not match it.
whyWrong.2: ACLs use the first match, not the most specific.

exhibit.title: Topology and port roles
exhibit.text:
PC1 10.1.1.10/24 -> R1 G0/0
R1 G0/1 -> R2 -> R3 G0/0
R3 G0/1 -> LAN C 10.3.3.0/24
R3 G0/2 -> LAN D 10.4.4.0/24
All routes and baseline connectivity are working.

prompt: A standard ACL denies source 10.1.1.10 and permits all else. PC1 must be blocked only from reaching LAN C, not R3 itself or LAN D. Where do you apply it?
options: R1 G0/0 inbound
R1 G0/1 outbound
R3 G0/1 outbound
R3 G0/0 inbound
explanation: A standard ACL sees only the source, so the attachment point sets the destination. R3 G0/1 outbound is the path into LAN C only.

whyWrong.0: R1 G0/0 inbound would block PC1 to every destination.
whyWrong.1: R1 G0/1 outbound would also block PC1's traffic to R3 and LAN D.
whyWrong.3: R3 G0/0 inbound would also block traffic to R3 itself and LAN D.

prompt: An extended ACL must block only TCP destination port 23 from PC1 to SRV. Following the placement guideline, where should it go?
options: R2 inbound on the transit link
R3 G0/1 outbound
R1 G0/0 inbound
R1 G0/1 inbound
explanation: Extended ACLs are placed close to the source, so the traffic is dropped before it crosses the network. That is R1 G0/0 inbound.

whyWrong.0: R2 inbound is farther from the source.
whyWrong.1: R3 G0/1 outbound is next to the destination, which is the guideline for standard ACLs.
whyWrong.3: Requests leave R1 G0/1; they do not enter it.

exhibit.title: Representative named ACL
exhibit.text:
10 permit tcp any host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
20 deny ip any host 10.100.20.20
30 permit ip any any

prompt: On IOS supporting sequence editing, which action removes only sequence 20 from named extended ACL CLIENTS-IN?
options: Use no access-list CLIENTS-IN 20 in global mode
Enter CLIENTS-IN configuration mode and use no 20
Enter CLIENTS-IN configuration mode and use delete 20
Use ip access-list resequence CLIENTS-IN 20 10
explanation: Enter `ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN` and then `no 20` to remove that one entry.

whyWrong.0: That is not the syntax for deleting a named ACL entry.
whyWrong.2: There is no `delete` command in ACL mode; use `no`.
whyWrong.3: `resequence` renumbers entries and does not delete any.

exhibit.title: Representative WEB-ONLY ACL
exhibit.text:
10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 eq www host 10.100.20.20
20 deny ip any any

prompt: The ACL is inbound on the client-facing interface. A client sends from TCP port 51000 to WEB port 80. Why is the request denied?
options: The permit tests source port 80 rather than destination port 80
The server's reply requires source port 51000 instead of 80
The final deny overrides a permit even when all fields match
The www alias matches a different service than numeric port 80
explanation: `eq www` comes right after the source address, so it tests the source port. The packet's source port is 51000, so the permit misses and deny 20 matches.

whyWrong.1: The question is about the request, whose source port is 51000 and destination port 80.
whyWrong.2: A matching permit ends evaluation, so the deny does not override it.
whyWrong.3: `www` is an alias for TCP port 80.

prompt: What sources match access-list 1 permit 10.100.10.0 255.255.255.0?
options: Any IPv4 source whose fourth octet is zero
Only source address 10.100.10.0
Exactly the addresses in 10.100.10.0/24
No sources because noncontiguous wildcards are invalid
explanation: IOS reads `255.255.255.0` as a wildcard, so the first three octets are ignored and the fourth must be 0. Any address ending in .0, such as 192.0.2.0, matches.

whyWrong.1: A single host needs wildcard 0.0.0.0 or `host`.
whyWrong.2: IOS reads the value as a wildcard, not as a subnet mask.
whyWrong.3: Wildcard bits need not be contiguous.

prompt: Which single ACE matches a UDP DNS query from a client using source port 51000 to server 10.1.1.53 on destination port 53?
options: permit tcp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 53
permit udp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 67
permit udp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 53
permit udp any eq 53 host 10.1.1.53
explanation: The query is UDP, and the service port 53 is the destination port, so `eq 53` goes after the destination host.

whyWrong.0: A TCP entry does not match a UDP packet.
whyWrong.1: UDP 67 is DHCP.
whyWrong.3: This tests source port 53, but the client's source port is 51000.

prompt: Which pair correctly predicts the first match for both packets?
options: A matches 10; B matches 30
A matches 20; B matches 30
A matches 20; B matches 40
A matches 10; B matches 20
explanation: Packet A misses the HTTPS permit and matches the deny for the first /26. Packet B is outside that /26 but inside the /24 HTTP permit.

whyWrong.2: Packet B matches entry 30, so it never reaches 40.
whyWrong.3: Packet A misses entry 10, and B is outside the deny's /26.

exhibit.title: DNS request and reply endpoints (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Query: 10.34.0.10 UDP/51000 -> 10.34.8.53 UDP/53
Reply: 10.34.8.53 UDP/53 -> 10.34.0.10 UDP/51000
Filter: R1 server-facing interface inbound

prompt: Which ACE narrowly permits the displayed UDP reply?
options: permit udp host 10.34.8.53 host 10.34.0.10 eq 53
permit udp host 10.34.8.53 eq 53 host 10.34.0.10 eq 51000
permit udp host 10.34.0.10 eq 51000 host 10.34.8.53 eq 53
permit tcp host 10.34.8.53 eq 53 host 10.34.0.10 eq 51000
explanation: The reply reverses the query: its source port is 53 and its destination is the client's port 51000. This entry matches that one packet and does not track sessions.

whyWrong.0: This requires destination port 53 on the client.
whyWrong.2: This describes the query direction.
whyWrong.3: The reply is UDP, not TCP.

prompt: An inbound ACL permit counter rises for a new HTTP request, but R1 has no route to its destination. What does the permit show?
options: The permit creates a temporary route to the destination
The request passed this filter; forwarding still needs a route
The HTTP session completed because the entry matched
The permit bypasses subsequent forwarding and filtering checks
explanation: A permit means only that this ACL did not drop the packet. Forwarding still needs a route, and an ACL cannot supply one.

whyWrong.0: An ACL permit does not install a route.
whyWrong.2: A matching request does not show a response arrived.
whyWrong.3: The packet still goes through routing and any other filters.

prompt: Which addresses match the source pair 10.34.0.77 0.0.0.31? Choose two.
explanation: The wildcard ignores the low five bits of the fourth octet, so the base 77 matches the block .64 to .95. The third octet must match exactly.

whyWrong.3: 96 starts the next block.
whyWrong.4: The third octet is compared exactly and must be 0.

prompt: A policy must permit client DNS queries to 10.34.8.53 over both UDP and TCP and deny everything else. Which two entries are required? Choose two.
options: permit tcp 10.34.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.34.8.53 established
explanation: DNS uses both UDP and TCP, and each needs its own entry with destination port 53. A broad `permit ip` would allow more than DNS.

whyWrong.2: This matches source port 53, not the query's destination port.
whyWrong.3: A new TCP connection starts with a SYN that has no ACK or RST, so `established` would not match it.
whyWrong.4: This permits other services to the DNS host.

prompt: Two hosts with correct /24 masks share VLAN 10 and talk through a Layer 2 switch. An ACL is inbound on the router's VLAN 10 interface. Why does it not block their traffic?
options: A standard ACL automatically permits all same-subnet addresses
ARP removes the ACL attachment after resolving a local neighbor
Inbound lists inspect only packets destined for the router itself
The hosts exchange those frames without traversing the router interface
explanation: Hosts in the same subnet reach each other directly through the switch. Their frames never cross the router interface, so its ACL never sees them.

whyWrong.0: There is no automatic same-subnet permit; the packets simply bypass the router.
whyWrong.1: ARP does not change an ACL attachment.
whyWrong.2: An inbound ACL checks transit traffic as well as traffic for the router.

exhibit.title: ACL counter comparison (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Same ACL, same attachment, no counter reset or reload:
HTTP permit: before 70, after 80
Explicit deny: before 12, after 12
Only the controlled client generated matching test traffic.

prompt: What does this before-and-after counter comparison show?
options: The permit increase establishes receipt of the server response
Exactly ten HTTP transactions completed during the test
The unchanged deny proves the whole path permits traffic
Ten new packets matched; application success remains unverified
explanation: The permit counter rose by ten and the deny did not, so ten packets matched the permit. This does not count transactions or show a response arrived.

whyWrong.0: A request-side match does not show a response was received.
whyWrong.1: One transaction can produce several matching packets.
whyWrong.2: These counters do not cover other interfaces or filters.

exhibit.title: Forward and return evidence (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Clients: 10.34.0.0/24; DNS: 10.34.8.53
Client-facing inbound ACL permits UDP and TCP queries to DNS port 53.
Server-facing inbound ACL:
 10 permit tcp 10.34.8.0 0.0.0.255 10.34.0.0 0.0.0.255 established
 20 deny ip any any
Capture: fresh UDP query reaches DNS; DNS sends reply to client port 51000.
R1 sees that reply on its server interface; deny 20 increases.
Policy: allow those DNS replies; retain the denial of other server-initiated traffic.

prompt: Which narrow change restores the service and keeps the stated restrictions?
options: Permit UDP replies from DNS source port 53 before the server-side deny
Replace the client-side deny with permit ip any any
Permit TCP destination port 53 on the server-side inbound list
Remove the server-side list because the client list is restrictive
explanation: The UDP DNS reply, with source port 53, misses the TCP-only return permit and hits the deny. Add a permit for UDP replies from port 53 ahead of the deny.

whyWrong.1: The request already passes, and `permit ip any any` is far too broad.
whyWrong.2: The missing packet is a UDP reply with source port 53, not a TCP request.
whyWrong.3: Removing the list drops the server-to-client restriction.

exhibit.title: A constrained policy change (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Active CLIENTS-IN:
10 permit tcp 10.34.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.34.8.20 eq 80
20 deny ip 10.34.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.34.8.20
30 permit ip any any
Change requirements: retain HTTP for all clients; add HTTPS only for admin 10.34.0.10; continue denying other client traffic to WEB.

prompt: Which proposed insertion meets all three access requirements?
options: Insert permit ip host 10.34.0.10 any at sequence 5
Insert permit tcp host 10.34.0.10 host 10.34.8.20 eq 443 at sequence 15
Append permit tcp host 10.34.0.10 host 10.34.8.20 eq 443 at sequence 40
Replace deny 20 with permit ip 10.34.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.34.8.20
explanation: The admin's HTTPS permit must go before deny 20, and only for that host and port. This grants the exception without opening WEB to other clients or services.

whyWrong.0: This permits all of the admin's protocols to anywhere.
whyWrong.2: Appended after sequence 40, the packet hits deny 20 first.
whyWrong.3: This permits all client traffic to WEB, not just the one exception.

exhibit.title: Safe replacement requirements (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Change constraints:
- Classic IOS interface behavior from this chapter
- Working console session retained
- Existing LIVE ACL ends with deny ip any any
- Add one approved management source while preserving other restrictions
- No deliberate unfiltered interval; fresh-session acceptance required

prompt: Which change procedure keeps the filtering policy and the console recovery path?
options: Delete LIVE first, then recreate it while its interface reference remains
Detach LIVE, verify management from the console, then construct NEXT
Append the new exception after LIVE's final deny and test only an existing session
Build and inspect NEXT in full, replace the reference, then test approved and denied flows
explanation: Build and check the full replacement ACL first, then switch the interface reference to it and test both the allowed and denied traffic. Keep the old list for rollback.

whyWrong.0: Deleting LIVE while it is attached leaves a gap in filtering.
whyWrong.1: Detaching LIVE leaves the interface unfiltered.
whyWrong.2: The appended exception sits after the final deny and never matches, and an existing session is not a fresh test.

exhibit.title: Two interface filters on one request path (exercise)
exhibit.text:
PC 10.34.0.10 -> WEB 10.34.8.20 TCP/80.
Approved policy permits this HTTP service and blocks other client traffic to WEB.
R1 G0/0 inbound CLIENTS-IN: HTTP permit increases during a fresh test.
R1 G0/1 outbound OLD-SERVERS: deny ip host 10.34.0.10 any increases during that test.
WEB HTTP was verified locally; connected routes and both links remain working.

prompt: The correct inbound permit matches the request, but it still fails. What is the next action without broadening the policy?
options: Inspect and reconcile the remaining outbound ACL with the approved HTTP policy
Change only the inbound permit to permit ip any any
Remove both ACLs because ping works from R1
Reset the HTTP server because an inbound permit proves end-to-end delivery
explanation: The request passes the inbound permit but then hits an explicit deny in the outbound ACL. Fix that outbound list, because a permit in one ACL cannot override a deny in another.

whyWrong.1: The request already matches the inbound permit, so widening it does not fix the outbound deny.
whyWrong.2: A ping from the router does not test this host's TCP path, and removing both ACLs drops the policy.
whyWrong.3: An inbound permit does not show end-to-end delivery.

prompt: Where should a standard ACL be placed?
options: Close to the destination
Close to the source
On the loopback interface
On the VTY lines only
explanation: A standard ACL matches only the source, so place it close to the destination. Extended ACLs go close to the source.

whyWrong.1: Close to the source is the guideline for extended ACLs.
whyWrong.2: A loopback sees no transit traffic.
whyWrong.3: VTY lines filter management sessions only.

prompt: Which command shows which ACL is applied to an interface and in which direction?
options: show ip interface
show access-lists
show running-config | include ip
show ip route
explanation: `show ip interface` lists the inbound and outbound ACLs on an interface. `show access-lists` shows the entries and match counts.

whyWrong.1: `show access-lists` shows entries and counters, not where they are applied.
whyWrong.2: That output does not show the applied ACL or its direction clearly.
whyWrong.3: The routing table shows routes, not ACLs.

prompt: What wildcard mask does the keyword `any` stand for?
explanation: `any` is 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255, so every address bit is ignored. `host` uses wildcard 0.0.0.0.

whyWrong.1: 0.0.0.0 is the wildcard for `host`.
whyWrong.3: 255.255.255.0 ignores only the first three octets.

prompt: Does an outbound ACL on a router filter packets the router generates itself?
options: No
Yes, always
Only ICMP packets
Only when the ACL is numbered
explanation: An outbound ACL does not filter packets that the router itself originates. It filters only traffic passing through the router.

whyWrong.1: Router-generated packets are not filtered by an outbound ACL.
whyWrong.2: No protocol is an exception.
whyWrong.3: Numbered and named ACLs behave the same.
